messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 42
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Oceania
  relationship_status: In a relationship
  occupation: Electrician
  trauma_type: Assault
  pcl5: 78

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Time of Day: The same time of day the event occurred, Dissociative Feeling: Beginning to feel detached or unreal, Auditory (Door): Doors opening or slamming
  Maladaptive Strategies: Screen Escape: I spend long hours on my phone, games, or internet to avoid thinking, Substance Use: I drink alcohol, take medication or use drugs, Avoid Media: Watching TV programmes/ films or reading about similar events
  Threat: Startle to Movement: Unexpected movement nearby causes me to react as if I am in danger, Startle to Touch: I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly, Avoid Unfamiliar Places: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger
  Memory: Snapshot Memory: I remember the frightening event as a few moments, and each moment is a picture in my mind., Guilt on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense guilt, Incomplete Picture: I feel like I am only remembering parts of what happened and the rest is missing
  Negative Appraisals: Character Blame: The event happened to me because of the sort of person I am, Hopelessness: I have no future, Self-Comparison: Somebody else would not have gotten into this situation

Vignette:
For Marcus, the assault happened on a Tuesday evening, just after seven o’clock. He had been finishing a wiring job in a basement unit of a new apartment complex, the only electrician still on site as the light outside shifted from grey to dusk. He remembered the foreman leaving, the heavy metal door clicking shut, and then the sound of it opening again too fast. Two men he did not know came through, and within seconds the job had stopped being about conduit and circuits. He could not say now exactly how long it lasted, or what was said. What stayed with him were snapshots: the overhead fluorescent light flickering, the concrete floor cold against his cheek, the door slamming once more after they left. The rest of the hour was gone, a stretch of time that felt like a missing page in a book he was supposed to have read.

In the weeks that followed, Marcus began to notice that the day itself had become a trap. Seven o’clock in the evening arrived like a scheduled dread. He would find himself glancing at his watch, his chest tightening, a sense of unreality creeping in as though he were watching his own hands from somewhere far away. He had always been steady on the job, known for keeping his cool, but now a door opening in the house—even his own front door, even when his girlfriend came home—made him flinch. He would freeze, his breath shallow, before he could tell himself it was just her. The same thing happened with unexpected movement: a colleague stepping into his peripheral vision on a job site, a dog rounding a corner too quickly. His body reacted before his mind caught up, heart hammering, muscles braced for impact. Touch was worse. A hand on his shoulder from behind could send him spinning, his hands up, his voice sharp. He had started to avoid new job sites altogether, telling his supervisor he preferred repeat work, familiar buildings where he already knew the layout, the exits, the people.

At home, Marcus spent hours on his phone. He scrolled through videos, played games, clicked from one thing to the next until his eyes burned. It was not about enjoyment. It was about keeping his mind occupied, filling the silence so the snapshots could not surface. He drank most nights now, enough to blur the edges, and he had stopped watching any show or film that involved violence, conflict, or even tense confrontation. He would check the description first, and if it seemed too close, he turned it off. His girlfriend had noticed. She did not say much, but he saw her watching him, and he knew she was trying to understand why he had become so jumpy, so distant, so quick to be alone.

What gnawed at him most was not the fear itself, but the guilt. When he remembered the assault—those few frozen moments that played over and over—he felt a hot, sick shame. He was certain that somebody else would not have gotten into that situation. Somebody more alert, more capable, more aware. The event had happened to him, he had come to believe, because of the sort of person he was. Someone weak. Someone who did not see it coming. Someone who deserved it, maybe, in some way he could not fully articulate. He had no future now. That was the thought that sat underneath everything else, quiet and absolute. There was no point planning, no point hoping. The person he had been before that Tuesday evening was gone, and he did not know how to build another version of himself.

What finally brought Marcus to seek help was a small thing, or felt like one. He had been asked to take on a straightforward rewiring job at a new house across town, and he had said no. He had made up an excuse about being overbooked, but the real reason was that he did not know the building, did not know the neighbourhood, did not know where the doors led. After he hung up, he sat in his truck for a long time, the engine off, the evening light fading, and he thought about how small his world had become. He was afraid of what he was turning into. He was afraid that if he did not change something, he would disappear entirely into the gaps and the snapshots and the hours spent staring at a screen. He did not know if therapy could fix him. He was not sure he deserved to be fixed. But he had come anyway, because the alternative—letting the missing pieces stay missing—felt worse.
